name: Green coffee bean extract

card.summary: Unroasted-coffee chlorogenic acid pill sold for fat loss; the best-known supporting study was retracted and the FTC acted against marketers.
card.aka: GCE, green coffee extract, chlorogenic acid supplement
card.note: Weight-loss marketing led to FTC settlements in 2014-2015; human trials are small and of poor quality per reviews.

quick.overview:
Green coffee bean extract is made from unroasted coffee beans, which are rich in chlorogenic acid. It is sold in capsule form as a fat-burning and appetite supplement.

A 2011 meta-analysis found tentative weight-loss effects but poor evidence quality, and a 2017 review concluded human studies were too poor to draw conclusions. A widely cited 2012 trial was retracted in 2014, and US regulators took action against several marketers.
quick.mechanism: Chlorogenic acid is proposed to slow carbohydrate absorption and change fat and glucose metabolism; animal studies in mice reported less fat accumulation on diets containing the extract. Human mechanisms have not been firmly established.
quick.risks: Trials in people with mild hypertension reported blood pressure effects with the extract and no major adverse events in small samples. Products contain varying amounts of chlorogenic acid and sometimes caffeine. The supplement is sold as a dietary supplement rather than a licensed drug.

lead: Green coffee bean extract (GCE) is a concentrate of unroasted coffee beans, standardised in supplements to chlorogenic acid, a polyphenol that is largely lost in roasting. [1][2] It has been sold as a weight-loss supplement and studied for blood pressure and metabolic markers. [3][4]

Wikipedia states that clinical evidence is insufficient to show that it works or is safe for weight loss. A 2011 systematic review of randomised trials found tentative evidence of weight loss but of poor quality, and a 2017 review of chlorogenic acid concluded that human studies were of poor quality and no conclusions could be drawn. [2][1]

The extract was promoted on The Dr. Oz Show in 2012, and in 2014-2015 the US Federal Trade Commission took action against several marketers, including settlements with Applied Food Sciences, which had sponsored the main trial cited in advertising. [2]

paras: GCE is sold as a fat-loss and appetite supplement and has been tested in small trials for blood pressure in people with mild hypertension and in metabolic syndrome. [3][4][5] The extract is also used in the Swiss water process for decaffeinating coffee. [2]

Chlorogenic acids are the main phenolic compounds of coffee, and reviews describe effects on biomarkers of chronic disease in animals and humans. [1] A thermogenic-agents review lists green coffee extract among natural weight-management ingredients. [6] In mice fed a standard or high-fat diet, green coffee extract was reported to reduce fat accumulation and weight gain. [7][8]

Wikipedia cites a 2011 meta-analysis (Onakpoya, Terry and Ernst) reporting tentative weight loss with poor evidence quality, and a 2017 review concluding human studies could not support conclusions. [2][1] A 2018 randomised trial in people with metabolic syndrome examined green coffee extract on body measurements, glycaemic control, blood pressure, lipids, insulin resistance and appetite. [4]
Small trials in mild hypertension reported blood pressure reductions with the extract in Japanese and other cohorts. [9][5][10]
The Dr. Oz Show featured green coffee extract in April and September 2012. A trial of the extract was retracted in 2014. [2]

In May 2014 the FTC charged the makers of Pure Green Coffee with deceptive claims, saying reliance on the study was deceptive because of serious flaws. In September 2014 Applied Food Sciences settled, and a guest who promoted the supplement on the show settled in January 2015. At a June 2014 Senate hearing Dr. Oz said he believed in the products as short-term aids but accepted they did not meet scientific proof standards. [2]

A 2006 randomised placebo-controlled trial in 28 people with mild hypertension examined chlorogenic acid from GCE for blood pressure and safety. [9] A 2018 randomised trial studied GCE in metabolic syndrome. [4] Registered trials have enrolled overweight adults (n=105) and people with metabolic syndrome (n=160). [11][12] Systematic reviews describe the human literature as poor quality for weight loss. [1][2]

timeline.event: Green coffee extract featured on The Dr. Oz Show. [2]
Main weight-loss trial retracted; FTC charges against marketers and Applied Food Sciences. [2]
FTC settlement with promoter linked to the TV segments. [2]
Review concludes human studies on chlorogenic acid too poor for conclusions. [1]
